title: Cross-Entropy Loss
body:
[[Loss Function]] that assigns a truth value
Implementation for [[Log Loss]]

---

[[Cross-Entropy]] used as the training objective for [[Classification]]. Evan's second line is the
important one: **this and [[Log Loss]] are the same function**, named from the information side and
the likelihood side respectively.

For one training example with true class $c$ and predicted distribution $\mathbf{q}$ over $k$
classes:

$$
L = -\sum_{i=1}^{k} p_i \log q_i = -\log q_c
$$

The collapse to a single term is the trick worth seeing. The true "distribution" $\mathbf{p}$ for a
labelled example is one-hot: probability 1 on the correct class, 0 on everything else. Every term
of the sum is multiplied by zero except the correct one, so **the loss is just the negative log of
the probability the model gave to the right answer.** Confident and right costs nothing; confident
and wrong costs a great deal. The binary case is
$-[y\log q + (1-y)\log(1-q)]$, which is [[Log Loss]] written out.

The total loss is the mean of that over the batch, which makes it an estimate of
$H(P,Q)$ over the data distribution. Minimising it minimises [[KL Divergence]] between the model
and the truth, since $H(P)$ is constant; [[KL Divergence]] carries that derivation.

## Why not squared error on the probabilities

You could, and it trains badly. Two reasons:

- **The gradient.** Paired with a [[Sigmoid]] or softmax [[Output Layer]], the cross-entropy
  gradient at the output simplifies to $q - y$, the plain difference between predicted and true.
  The activation's derivative cancels out, so a confidently wrong unit gets a *large* gradient.
  With squared error that derivative survives, and a confidently wrong sigmoid unit is deep in its
  flat region, so it gets almost no gradient exactly when it most needs one. See [[Sigmoid]].
- **The penalty shape.** $-\log q \to \infty$ as $q \to 0$, so assigning near-zero probability to
  what actually happened is unboundedly bad. Squared error caps that penalty at 1.

Regression is the other way round: squared error there, because a [[Vector Norm]] of the residual
is the right thing to measure. [[Loss Function]] carries the general comparison.

Practical note: implementations fuse the softmax and the log into one operation, both for numerical
stability (no $\log 0$) and because the fused gradient is the simple $q - y$ above.

## Related

- [[Log Loss]]: the same function, the binary case, named from likelihood
- [[Cross-Entropy]], [[KL Divergence]], [[Shannon Entropy]]: where the formula comes from
- [[Loss Function]], [[Gradient Descent]], [[Back Propagation]]
- [[Output Layer]], [[Sigmoid]]: what it is paired with
- [[Vector Norm]] ([[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]): the losses that *are* norms,
  which this is not
